engagement.coverage_declaration: Only the findings that match an advisory already published upstream are reproduced here. The others are withheld pending a disclosure decision.

findings.title: Any certificate id sent in `replacements` silently disables expiry notification and auto-rotation on another owner's certificate

location.component: CertificatesUpload.post (same defect on CertificatesList.post:396 and Certificates.put:849)

findings.evidence: Source: three write schemas accept a list of certificate ids from the request body - CertificateInputSchema.replaces/replacements (schemas.py:82-85), CertificateEditInputSchema.replaces/replacements (schemas.py:188-191) and CertificateUploadInputSchema.replaces (schemas.py:402); the pre_load hooks at schemas.py:146-151 and 194-199 copy `replacements` into `replaces`. Transformation: the three handlers pass the loaded value straight through - views.py:666 `return service.upload(**data)`, views.py:543 `cert = service.create(**data)`, views.py:997 `cert = service.update(certificate_id, **data)` (service.update is a blind `setattr` loop, service.py:377-378; Certificate.__init__ assigns the collection at models.py:218). Sink: `@event.listens_for(Certificate.replaces, "append")` at models.py:506-516 mutates the *appended* row, not the caller's row: `value.notify = False`. Nothing between the request and that event authorizes the appended id - a grep for `replaces|replacement|replaced` over the four audited files returns no permission check of any kind, while every sibling operation on a foreign certificate does check (CertificatePermission at views.py:942, 1097, 1154, 1270, 1592, 1677, 1754, 1829). Second-order effects of the same association, all in the audited scope: `not_(Certificate.replaced.any())` removes the victim from auto-reissue (service.py:277), from expiration metrics (service.py:1431), from the expiring-deployed-certificate checks (service.py:181, 214, 223) and from GET /certificates/valid (service.py:762). Cheapest entry point is the upload handler: it needs only StrictRolePermission (views.py:651), a `body` and an `owner` (schemas.py:389-403) - no authority permission, no private key, no domain authorization.
findings.impact: An authenticated caller who can reach any of the three write endpoints can name any certificate id in the system in `replacements` and, in one request, turn off that certificate's expiration notification, exclude it from auto-rotation and hide it from the valid-certificate query and the expiry metrics - without touching the row through any endpoint that would have checked ownership. The victim's certificate then expires with no warning to its owner and no automated renewal, which in a certificate-management service is a production outage delivered on a timer. The ids are sequential integers, so the same request repeated over a range disables the notification path for the whole inventory.
findings.preconditions: A valid account that passes StrictRolePermission (views.py:651) - the weakest of the three entry points is POST /certificates/upload, which requires only a parseable certificate body and an owner string. The victim certificate id must be known or guessed; ids are dense integers and GET /certificates lists them to any authenticated user.
findings.recommendation: Authorize every element of `replaces` the same way the handlers already authorize the certificate named in the URL: resolve each replaced certificate and require the caller to be its creator or to hold CertificatePermission over it, rejecting the whole request otherwise. Put the check in the view layer next to the existing CertificatePermission blocks (or in a shared helper called by all three handlers) rather than in the schema, so the rule is visible where the other authorization decisions are made. Independently, the `Certificate.replaces` append event at models.py:506 mutates a row the caller may not own as a side effect of an ORM assignment; making that mutation explicit in the rotation code path (service.reissue_certificate, which is the legitimate producer of a replacement link at service.py:1027-1028) would remove the ambient authority entirely.
findings.inference: That AssociatedCertificateSchema (lemur/schemas.py, outside the audited directory) resolves an arbitrary certificate id supplied in the request body into a Certificate instance without any owner or permission check of its own. Every sibling association in this module behaves that way and no audited file performs the check, but the resolver itself was not read.

triage.reason: The replacement link is intended: service.reissue_certificate sets `primitives["replaces"] = [certificate]` (service.py:1027-1028) for the certificate being rotated. What is not bounded is the id source - on the HTTP paths the id comes from the request body with no relation to the caller's certificate, and the mutation lands on the foreign row (models.py:516).

A second principal is explicit in this module: certificates carry `owner`, `user_id` and `roles`, and the same file gates every other cross-certificate operation with CertificatePermission (views.py:942 and seven further sites).
The affected state is another owner's certificate lifecycle - notify flag, rotation eligibility, expiry metrics - which is the core function of this service, not incidental data.

findings.limits: Establishes the write path and the state change; it does not establish how a given deployment reacts operationally to `notify = False` (whether some other notification channel outside this module still warns the owner), and it does not establish who exactly passes StrictRolePermission, whose definition is outside the audited directory.

findings.title: Destination plugin option values, including the SFTP password and private key passphrase, are serialized to every authenticated caller
findings.evidence: DestinationOutputSchema declares `options = fields.List(fields.Dict())` (schemas.py:28) — the raw JSON column of the model (models.py:20, `options = Column(JSONType)`), dumped with no allowlist and no per-key filter. Its `@post_dump fill_object` then copies the same list a second time into the nested plugin object: `data["plugin"]["pluginOptions"] = data["options"]` (schemas.py:33), and for options whose type contains `export-plugin` it also unfolds the nested plugin's own option list into the response (schemas.py:34-36). The stored values are exactly what an admin submitted at creation time: views.py:188 forwards `data["plugin"]["plugin_options"]` into `service.create`. For a destination backed by the SFTP plugin, that option list contains `password` (plugin.py:62-68) and `privateKeyPass` (plugin.py:76-82), both declared `"type": "str"` with no marker distinguishing them from a non-secret option such as a port or an account number; the plugin's own module docstring states "Passwords are not encrypted and stored as a plain text" (plugin.py:13). Both read handlers that emit this schema are guarded only by `AuthenticatedResource`: `GET /destinations` (views.py:36-37) and `GET /destinations/<int:destination_id>` (views.py:198-199) carry no `admin_permission`, while `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on the same resources do (views.py:101-102, 253-254, 348). The resource docstrings document the option `value` travelling in the response body (views.py:59-87, 221-246). Secret values themselves are [REDACTED:secret] — none appear literally in the code, only the field names that carry them.
findings.impact: Any principal holding a valid session or token for the API — including the lowest-privilege read-only account, which is not allowed to create or modify a destination — can read back, in cleartext, the transport credentials of every configured destination: the SFTP host, port and user, the account password and the passphrase of the RSA private key, and, for export-plugin options, the nested plugin's own option values (export passphrases). Those credentials authenticate to the hosts where certificates and their private keys are deployed, and the SFTP plugin's default user is `root` (plugin.py:55-61), so the exposure converts an ordinary API account into a foothold on the destination infrastructure. The exposure is silent and repeatable: it happens on a routine listing call, so it leaves no trace distinguishable from normal UI traffic, and it survives any hiding of the fields in the frontend, since the data has already left the server.
findings.preconditions: A valid authenticated session or token of any role; at least one destination configured with a plugin whose option list contains a secret (the SFTP plugin in scope, or any export plugin reached through the nested `export-plugin` branch).
findings.recommendation: Stop dumping the stored option blob. Give plugin options an explicit secret marker in the option contract (for example a `"type": "password"` or a `"secret": true` flag, which the SFTP `password` and `privateKeyPass` entries would carry), and have DestinationOutputSchema emit an allowlist of non-secret keys, replacing the value of a marked option with a placeholder on the way out — in the same place that today copies the list into `plugin.pluginOptions`, so both copies are covered by one control. Keep write access to the real value server-side only, and add a regression test that dumps a destination holding a marked option and fails if the value appears anywhere in the serialized response, including under the nested plugin. Rotate any credential that has been readable through this route.

triage.reason: The only layer that could strip the field after `fill_object` is a parent-class hook in `LemurOutputSchema` or the `validate_schema` decorator, both in lemur/common/schema.py, which is outside the audited directory and was not read. Within scope there is no redaction: the option dicts carry no field that would let a generic filter tell a password from a port (plugin.py:40-98), and the resource docstrings document option values in the response body (views.py:59-87).

A second principal exists and is named in the same file: the admin who writes the destination and its credentials (guarded by `admin_permission`, views.py:101-102, 253-254, 348) versus any authenticated non-admin who reads it (views.py:36-37, 198-199, 360-361).
The data is authentication material for a remote host: `password` and `privateKeyPass` options of the SFTP destination plugin (plugin.py:62-82), consumed by `ssh.connect` (plugin.py:119-127).

findings.inference: That `service.get` and `service.render` return `Destination` instances whose `options` attribute is the column written by `service.create` from `data["plugin"]["plugin_options"]`, and that neither `validate_schema` nor `LemurOutputSchema` removes the `options` key after `fill_object` runs. Both live outside the audited directory (lemur/destinations/service.py, lemur/common/schema.py) and were not read. The `@post_dump` body is itself strong in-scope evidence that the key is present at dump time — `data["plugin"]["pluginOptions"] = data["options"]` would raise otherwise — but the final serialized body was never observed.
findings.limits: Establishes the exposure for `GET /destinations` and `GET /destinations/<id>`, which use `destinations_output_schema` (many) and `destination_output_schema` (single). It does not establish it for `GET /certificates/<id>/destinations`: that handler declares the single-object schema (views.py:360) while `service.render` returns a paginated collection, so what its response actually contains was not determined. It also does not establish which roles exist in the deployment, nor how many destinations use a secret-bearing plugin.

findings.title: Read verbs on the destinations resource are not gated by admin_permission while every write verb is
findings.evidence: The module imports `admin_permission` (views.py:14) and applies it to exactly three handlers: `DestinationsList.post` (views.py:102), `Destinations.put` (views.py:254) and `Destinations.delete` (views.py:348). The four read handlers inherit only `AuthenticatedResource` and carry no permission decorator: `DestinationsList.get` (views.py:36-37), `Destinations.get` (views.py:198-199), `CertificateDestinations.get` (views.py:360-361) and `DestinationsStats.get` (views.py:434). All four are registered on the public API blueprint (views.py:441-450). The asymmetry is inside one file: the same resource class treats its own object as admin-managed for writing and as world-readable-to-any-session for reading.
findings.impact: Any authenticated principal, whatever its role, enumerates the full destination inventory of the installation — labels, descriptions, plugin slugs, per-destination configuration and the statistics endpoint — for an object class the same module considers privileged enough that creating, modifying or deleting it requires an administrator. On its own this is reconnaissance of the certificate delivery topology (which hosts and services receive certificates, under which plugin). Combined with F-001, the same unprivileged call also returns the credentials of those hosts, which is why the two are reported separately: fixing either one reduces the impact of the other, and only fixing both closes the class.
findings.preconditions: A valid authenticated session or token of any role.
findings.recommendation: Decide the read policy explicitly rather than by omission, and apply it in one place: either require the same `admin_permission` on the read handlers, or introduce a declared read permission for operators and attach it to all four handlers, including `DestinationsStats.get`. Prefer deny-by-default at the resource level — a base class or a `method_decorators` list on the resource — so that adding a handler later does not silently ship unguarded, and add a route x method x role test matrix that fails when a destinations handler has no permission attached.

triage.reason: Whether `AuthenticatedResource` itself enforces a role, or whether a global filter re-checks permissions below the resource layer, is decided in lemur/auth/service.py and lemur/auth/permissions.py, outside the audited directory and not read. The in-scope evidence points the other way: if `AuthenticatedResource` already required an administrator, the explicit `admin_permission` on the three write handlers would be redundant.

Destinations are a global, admin-managed resource — the model has no owner or tenant column (models.py:16-22) — so every non-admin authenticated caller is a second principal with respect to the administrator who created the record.

findings.inference: That `AuthenticatedResource` authenticates without authorizing, i.e. that a non-admin session reaches these handlers. The class is defined outside the audited directory; the argument rests on the redundancy of `admin_permission` on the write handlers of the same resources.
findings.limits: Does not establish the role model of the deployment (how many roles exist, whether ordinary users are issued API tokens), and does not cover the read handlers of any other module.

findings.title: Migration tools let the model choose where the management token is sent (host, hostDelivery, proxy, headers)
findings.evidence: exportSpace.ts:99-109 declares `host` ('Management API host'), `hostDelivery` ('Delivery API host'), `proxy` ('HTTP/HTTPS proxy config'), `rawProxy` ('Pass raw proxy config directly to Axios') and `headers` (z.record(z.string())) as ordinary model-supplied tool parameters; importSpace.ts:69-86 declares the same `host`, `proxy`, `rawProxy` and `headers`. Both tool bodies then build one option bag out of the model's arguments and the operator's credential: `const exportOptions = { ...args, managementToken, ... } as any` (exportSpace.ts:134-140, mirrored at importSpace.ts:111-115), where `managementToken = createClientConfig(config).accessToken` (exportSpace.ts:126-127) - the CMA token that register.ts:21 read from CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_ACCESS_TOKEN. The bag is handed to the job unchanged (exportSpace.ts:148, importSpace.ts:119). The operator's own pinned host, `CONTENTFUL_HOST` (env.ts:9-13, default 'api.contentful.com', passed to the tools at register.ts:22), is never read by either tool: `config.host` appears nowhere in these two files, so `args.host` is not an override of the configured host, it is the only host these two tools have.
findings.impact: One sentence of text in any content the model reads - a CMS entry, an asset description, a tool result - can make the next migration call carry the operator's Contentful Management API token to a host, or through a proxy, that the text chose. A CMA token is not scoped to one space: it is the credential for everything its owner can reach in the organization, so the loss is durable and survives the session. `headers` additionally lets the model attach arbitrary headers to a credentialed request, and `proxy` accepts embedded credentials ('user:pass@host:port', importSpace.ts:73). This is the outbound leg that makes F-003 exploitable rather than merely wrong.
findings.preconditions: The workflow tool must be enabled (see F-006), and the model must have ingested attacker-authored text. No credential of the attacker's own is needed.
findings.recommendation: Delete `host`, `hostDelivery`, `proxy`, `rawProxy` and `headers` from both input schemas and take the transport from ContentfulConfig instead - `config.host` for the management host, one operator-configured proxy, no model-supplied headers. If a per-call host must remain, validate it against an operator-configured allowlist inside the tool body before it can reach the option bag, and never spread `...args` into a bag that also carries the token: build the bag field by field from a whitelist of parameters the model is allowed to influence.
findings.inference: That contentful-export and contentful-import send the Authorization bearer for `managementToken` to the `host`/`proxy` supplied in the same options object was read from the parameters' own descriptions ('Management API host', 'HTTP/HTTPS proxy config') and from the fact that the tool passes them for no other purpose; the libraries' source is outside the audited scope and was not read.

triage.reason: No layer between the schema and the request constrains the destination. The one control that does exist is narrower than it looks: `managementToken` is written after `...args` (exportSpace.ts:134-136), so the model cannot substitute its own token - it can only redirect ours.
These are declared MCP tool parameters; their values arrive as arguments a model produced after reading content it does not control, and no allowlist narrows them before the sink.

Two principals: the operator, who configured the CMA token in the server environment, and the author of the CMS content the agent reads, who is not the operator and who ends up choosing the endpoint the operator's token is presented to.

A deploying MCP client could show literal arguments and require per-call approval, which would bound this. No exported client configuration, ticket or written statement was provided with the target, and per FP-08 the absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

findings.limits: Does not establish that the token appears verbatim in a request to the attacker host - that step lives in contentful-export/contentful-import, which were not read. Does not establish which MCP client deploys this server or whether it gates tool calls.

findings.title: Hook-supplied tag and data-attribute values concatenated into markup and emitted verbatim
findings.evidence: Line 66 builds a tag string from hook output: tags.push(`span data-${prop[0]}="${prop[1]}"`). The hook is invoked with the pad itself (line 64), and the comment on lines 62-63 says the entries are 'tags stored as [tag, value]' - the second element is document data, not a plugin constant. That string is later written raw as the tag: emitOpenTag does assem.append('<'); assem.append(tags[i]); assem.append('>') (lines 179-182), and emitCloseTag mirrors it (lines 195-198). Core writes the quotes around prop[1] and escapes nothing between them, so a value containing '"' closes an attribute inside a tag core is assembling. The sibling hook exportHtmlAdditionalTags (lines 56-61) has the same shape: its entries become raw tag names on line 181.
findings.impact: Stored XSS in every HTML export of an affected pad on an instance running a plugin that feeds pad-derived values through this hook: the attacker adds an attribute (an event handler) or an entire tag to the exported document, which executes for whoever opens the export.
findings.preconditions: A plugin implementing exportHtmlAdditionalTagsWithData (or exportHtmlAdditionalTags) that returns values taken from the pad rather than fixed constants. No plugin source was in scope.
findings.recommendation: Stop passing a fragment of markup between core and plugins. Keep the hook's return value as structured data ([name, value]) all the way to the writer, validate the attribute name against '^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9-]*$' and escape the value with Security.escapeHTMLAttribute at the point where emitOpenTag writes it - the same treatment line 285 already gives an attribute value in this file.
findings.inference: That an installed plugin returns a value derived from pad content rather than a constant. The basis is the hook's own signature (it receives `pad`, line 64) and the comment describing the entries as tag/value pairs; no plugin implementation was readable in scope.

triage.reason: Between line 66 and the write on line 181 the string is only stored in the tags array; no control is applied at either end.

The value's origin is a plugin, and plugin code is outside the audited scope. If every implementation returned constants the finding would die - that could not be established, and 'the plugins probably behave' is exactly the FP-08 move triage.md forbids.
The sink is the tag itself: line 181 writes the string between '<' and '>', so both the attribute value and the tag name are structural.
There is no server-side equivalent control: this is the only place the exported tag is assembled.

findings.limits: Establishes a missing control in core, not that any shipped plugin exercises it. Severity assumes a plugin that passes pad data through the hook; with constant-only plugins the impact is nil.
